lec05kp03-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp03-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP02 turned XOR into three positions with two lines and separated them with the last layer. With more lines, is the last layer still enough?

lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-54.name: term:Score
lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-54.text:
Score: the number from plugging
a point into line i, gᵢ(x) = wᵢᵀx
+ bᵢ.

lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-55.name: term:Step rule
lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-55.text:
Step rule: a score above 0 gives
1, anything else 0 (exactly 0
also gives 0).

lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-56.name: term:Bit
lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-56.text:
Bit: 1 if the point is on the
positive side of a line (score
above 0), otherwise 0.

lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-57.name: term:Code
lec05kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp03-p1-57.text:
Code: the three bits of a point
written in a row, like its house
number.

lec05kp03-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp03-u01-p2-title.text: Three lines cut seven plots, each with its own code

lec05kp03-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp03-u01-p2-bridge.text: Each point gets three bits from three lines; the bits form its code, a corner of the cube. How many plots do three concrete lines cut the plane into?

lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-1.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p2|Input plane cut by three orange lines into seven colored plots labelled by code; g1=x1, g2=x2, g3=-x1+x2-1; example (1,1) has code 110.

lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-4.text: Three lines cut seven plots, each with its own code

lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-32.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p2#32
lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-32.text: The three lines and an example

lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-35.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p2#35
lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-35.text:
The coefficients are a teaching choice, not the original
figure's equations; arrows point to the positive side, and
points on a line get 0.

lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-36.name: term:Cell
lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-36.text:
Cell: all points that get the same code, together, form one
plot.

lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-40.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p2#40
lec05kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp03-p2-40.text: Bits 1, 1, 0 (−1 ≤ 0 gives 0), so the code is 110.

lec05kp03-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp03-u01-p3-title.text: No point receives 101: its three conditions contradict, so the plane has only 7 plots

lec05kp03-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp03-u01-p3-bridge.text: Three lines cut seven plots, each with its own code; three bits can write 8 codes but the plane has only 7 plots. Why can no point receive 101?

lec05kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp03-p3-1.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p3|Four panels: x1>0 right half, x2<=0 lower half, above the line g3, and all three stacked with empty intersection; definitions of realized and unrealized codes.

lec05kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp03-p3-36.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p3#36
lec05kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp03-p3-36.text:
① and ② give x₁ > 0 and x₂ ≤ 0, so x₂ ≤ 0 < x₁ + 1 and ③ cannot
hold. Three bits can write 8 codes, but the plane has only 7
plots.

lec05kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp03-p3-38.name: term:Realized code
lec05kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp03-p3-38.text:
Realized code: a code that at least one input point receives (7 of
them).

lec05kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp03-p3-39.name: term:Unrealized code
lec05kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp03-p3-39.text:
Unrealized code: a code that can be written but no input point
receives (101); it is not missing data.

lec05kp03-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp03-u01-p4-title.text: Codes as cube corners: the last layer is one cut, and q = 0 is a plane

lec05kp03-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp03-u01-p4-bridge.text: No point receives 101: its three conditions contradict, so the plane has only 7 plots. Put these codes in the cube: where does the output layer's cut go?

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-1.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4|Cube with eight corners colored like the plots, 101 hollow; definition of the output score q = a1y1 + a2y2 + a3y3 + a0 and the cut q = 0.

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-4.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4#4
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-4.text: The 8 codes are the cube's 8 corners

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-33.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4#33
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-33.text:
Corner colors match the plots of the previous page; 101 is hollow:
no input reaches it.

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-35.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4#35
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-35.text: The last layer is one cut

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-36.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4#36
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-36.text:
The 8 three-bit codes are exactly the coordinates (y₁, y₂, y₃)
of the cube's corners; the step rule outputs only corners and
never fills the inside.

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-37.name: term:Output score
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-37.text:
Output score: q(y) = a₁y₁ + a₂y₂ + a₃y₃ + a₀; q > 0 means A,
otherwise B.

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-40.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4#40
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-40.text: aᵢ is the vote of each bit and a₀ is the starting score.

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-42.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4#42
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-42.text:
q = 0 is a plane in the cube: it splits the corners
into two sides, which is one cut.

lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-44.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p4#44
lec05kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp03-p4-44.text:
The condition only has to hold for realized codes; a label
on the unrealized code changes no input's prediction.

lec05kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp03-p5-76.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p5#76

lec05kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp03-p5-77.name: term:Linearly separable
lec05kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp03-p5-77.text:
Linearly separable: all of A on one side of a plane and all of B on the
other.

lec05kp03-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp03-u01-p6-bridge.text: Score every corner: all A on one side and all B on the other, so the cut separates them. Cut back in the input plane, what does the A region look like?

lec05kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp03-p6-28.name: term:Union
lec05kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp03-p6-28.text:
Union: several regions joined into one. Class A is the

lec05kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp03-p6-29.name: term:Convex
lec05kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp03-p6-29.text:
Convex: for any two points of the region, the segment
between them stays inside.

lec05kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp03-p6-31.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p6#31

lec05kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp03-p6-35.name: fig:lec05-kp03-p6#35
lec05kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp03-p6-35.text:
Myth: two-layer networks only classify convex regions.
One code's region is convex, but the last layer can

lec05kp03-frame-u01.text: Codes of several lines and the limit of two-layer networks

steps.label: Codes of several lines and the limit of two-layer networks
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp03 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 11 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Two spaces
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP03. Prerequisites: the method of KP02 (each hidden line gives one bit, the bits form a code, and the output layer cuts once more on the code), the corners of a cube (three bits give 2 to the power 3, that is 8 combinations, exactly the coordinates of the 8 corners), and the fact that a plane splits space into two sides. This page lays out the tools: a score is the number obtained by plugging a point into a line; the step rule gives 1 for a score above 0 and 0 otherwise; a bit is 1 on the positive side of a line; and the three bits of a point in a row form its code. The three points in the figure land at the cube corners 110, 000 and 011 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the seven plots.

steps.label: Seven plots
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the two spaces. This page uses three concrete lines: g1 equals x1, g2 equals x2 and g3 equals minus x1 plus x2 minus 1; the coefficients are a teaching choice, not the equations of the original figure. A cell is all the points that get the same code, together forming one plot. For example the point (1,1) scores 1, 1, minus 1, so its bits are 1, 1, 0 (minus 1 is at most 0 and gives 0) and its code is 110. Seven codes occur and 101 does not (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the code 101.

steps.label: Code 101
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the seven plots. This page explains why no point receives 101. The code 101 needs three things at once: bit 1 is 1, that is x1 above 0; bit 2 is 0, that is x2 at most 0; bit 3 is 1, that is x2 above x1 plus 1. The first two make x2 at most 0 and below x1 plus 1, so the third cannot hold. A realized code is one that at least one input point receives, 7 in all; an unrealized code can be written but no input point receives it, here 101. This is not missing data: however many points are collected, 101 never appears (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the code cube.

steps.label: Code cube
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the code 101. This page treats codes as cube corners: the 8 three-bit codes are exactly the coordinates of the 8 corners, the corner colors match the plots of the previous page, and 101 is a hollow circle. The output score q equals a1 y1 plus a2 y2 plus a3 y3 plus a0, with q above 0 called A and otherwise B; a_i is the vote of each bit and a0 the starting score. q equal to 0 is a plane in the cube that splits the corners into two sides, which is one cut. The condition only has to hold for realized codes (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the corner scores.

steps.label: Corner scores
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the code cube. This page keeps the lecture's output formula q equal to minus y1 minus y2 plus y3 plus 0.5 and substitutes corner by corner: 000 gives 0.5, 001 gives 1.5 and 011 gives 0.5, all A; 010 and 100 give minus 0.5, 110 gives minus 1.5 and 111 gives minus 0.5, all B. The score of 101 is 0.5, but no input gets it, so classification is unaffected. A all on one side of a plane and B all on the other is called linearly separable (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the notch of region A.

steps.label: Notch of region A
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the corner scores. This page goes back to the plane. Class A is the union of the plots 000, 001 and 011, that is, several regions joined into one. Convex means that for any two points of the region the segment between them stays inside. Take P(minus 0.15, minus 1) and Q(minus 0.15, 2): both are in A, yet the segment PQ passes through R(minus 0.15, 0.62) of the B plot, so region A is not convex. A common myth says two-layer networks only classify convex regions: one code's region is convex but the last layer can accept several codes, whose union may have notches (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the second labelling.

steps.label: Second labelling
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the notch of region A. This page sets A to {000, 110, 111} and the rest to B. On the cube's bottom face y3 equal to 0 the four corners are: A at 000 and 110, B at 010 and 100, alternating along the diagonal. In the input plane these four corners are the four quadrants cut by the two coordinate axes, just like XOR in KP01: nonseparable, and a counterexample (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the shared midpoint.

steps.label: Shared midpoint
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the second labelling. This page gives the proof. Adding the two A corners: q(000) plus q(110) equals a0 plus (a1 plus a2 plus a0), that is a1 plus a2 plus 2 a0, which must be above 0. Adding the two B corners: q(010) plus q(100) equals (a2 plus a0) plus (a1 plus a0), the same a1 plus a2 plus 2 a0, which must be at most 0. One expression cannot be both above 0 and at most 0, a contradiction, so no a0, a1, a2 separates them. Geometrically the two diagonals meet at the midpoint M and, q being linear, q(M) is both the average of the two A scores and of the two B scores (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the extra layer.

steps.label: Extra layer
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the shared midpoint. This page explains that the network is not hopeless; this one cut is not enough. What is blocked is this fixed set of lines plus one cut, not every two-layer network: another set of lines gives other codes and other counterexamples. Any corner can be cut off alone by one plane: the plane y1 plus y2 minus y3 equal to 1.5 cuts off only 110, y1 plus y2 plus y3 equal to 2.5 only 111, and minus y1 minus y2 minus y3 equal to minus 0.5 only 000. One cut per target corner, with the results merged, recognises the whole A set, which is one more layer (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the hypercube.

steps.label: Extension: hypercube
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the extra layer. This page is the extension: the general form. With d input coordinates and p lines, the code y is the vector of f(g1(x)) to f(gp(x)), lying in {0,1} to the power p, which has 2 to the power p corners, the corners of a p-dimensional hypercube. A segment has 2 corners, a square 4 and a cube 8, doubling with every extra bit. This unit's example has d equal to 2 and p equal to 3 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the hypercube. Two exercises. Q1: 101 needs g1 equal to x1 above 0, g2 equal to x2 at most 0 and g3 above 0; the third gives x2 above x1 plus 1, above 1, which contradicts x2 at most 0, so no input gets 101 and assigning 101 to A or B changes no prediction. Q2: both sums are a1 plus a2 plus 2 a0; with y3 equal to 0, a3 times 0 is 0, so a3 drops out and the contradiction stays; with a1 equal to a2 equal to 0 and a0 equal to 1, all four corners score 1 and B is called A whatever a3 is (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
